rubric.why: The definition must state that heat is taken in from the surroundings.
rubric.description: Defines an endothermic reaction as one that absorbs heat from its surroundings.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the complete definition; 1 mark for stating that heat is absorbed without identifying its source.

modelAnswer: An endothermic reaction is a chemical reaction in which heat is absorbed from the surroundings.

items.followUp: Why do suspensions scatter a beam of light?

rubric.why: The Tyndall effect occurs because colloidal particles scatter light passing through a colloid.
rubric.description: Links the Tyndall effect to light scattering by colloidal particles.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for explaining both the particles and their scattering of light; 1 mark for naming the effect or stating only that light is scattered.

modelAnswer: Colloidal particles scatter a beam of light passing through a colloid.
This scattering of light is called the Tyndall effect.

items.followUp: Why is pure iron generally not used for making tools?

rubric.why: Pure gold is too soft for many uses, so it is commonly alloyed to make it harder and stronger.
rubric.description: States that pure gold is soft and explains why it is alloyed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying its softness and 1 mark for stating that it is alloyed to improve strength or hardness.

modelAnswer: Pure gold is very soft and is not strong enough for making durable ornaments or objects.
It is therefore mixed with other metals, such as copper, to make it harder and stronger.

rubric.why: The question asks for any four elements in Group 17, the halogens.
rubric.how: Award 0.5 mark for each correct halogen, up to 2 marks.

modelAnswer: Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are four halogens.

items.followUp: Write the equation for the reaction of methane with chlorine in diffused sunlight.

rubric.why: In bright sunlight, chlorine substitutes for one hydrogen atom in methane, forming chloromethane and hydrogen chloride.
rubric.description: Gives the balanced substitution reaction and its products.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct products and 1 mark for the balanced equation with sunlight indicated.

modelAnswer: In bright sunlight, methane reacts with chlorine by substitution.
CH₄ + Cl₂ ⟶ CH₃Cl + HCl

items.followUp: Write four differences between an element and a compound.

rubric.why: A compound's constituent elements are chemically combined in a definite proportion.
rubric.description: Contrasts the formation and composition of a compound with a mixture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that compounds form by chemical combination in a fixed ratio, unlike mixtures.

rubric.why: A compound has properties different from its constituent substances, while mixture components retain their properties.
rubric.description: Compares the properties of compounds and mixtures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving this contrast.

rubric.why: Compounds are separated by chemical methods; mixture components can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.description: Compares how compounds and mixtures are separated.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving this contrast.

rubric.why: A pure compound has characteristic fixed melting and boiling points; a mixture generally does not.
rubric.description: Contrasts the melting or boiling points of compounds and mixtures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct comparison of their characteristic melting or boiling points.

rubric.why: A compound has a definite composition; mixtures have variable composition and may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.
rubric.description: Compares the composition or uniformity of compounds and mixtures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct comparison of composition or physical uniformity.

modelAnswer: A compound is formed when elements chemically combine; a mixture is formed by physically mixing substances.
A compound has a fixed composition and its elements are present in a definite ratio; a mixture has a variable composition.
A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements; the components of a mixture retain their properties.
A compound can be separated into its elements by chemical methods; the components of a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
A pure compound has fixed melting and boiling points; a mixture generally does not have fixed melting and boiling points.

items.followUp: Explain the formation of a coordinate covalent bond in the ammonium ion, using a dot-and-cross diagram or a Lewis representation.

rubric.why: In a coordinate covalent bond, the shared pair of electrons is supplied by one atom.
rubric.description: Defines a coordinate covalent bond in terms of its shared electron pair.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one atom donates both electrons in the shared pair.

rubric.why: Ammonia donates its nitrogen lone pair to H⁺ to form NH₄⁺.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the donor, acceptor and ammonium-ion product.

rubric.why: Water donates an oxygen lone pair to H⁺ to form H₃O⁺.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the donor, acceptor and hydronium-ion product.

rubric.why: The examples should show formation of the coordinate bond and the resulting ion.
rubric.description: Shows a correct formation equation for at least one example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct equation or equivalent coordinate-bond representation for either example.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is formed when one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair to another atom.
In ammonia, nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺: NH₃ + H⁺ ⟶ NH₄⁺.
In water, oxygen donates a lone pair to H⁺: H₂O + H⁺ ⟶ H₃O⁺.
In each product, the donated pair forms a coordinate covalent bond.

items.followUp: What are isotopes? Describe the isotopes of oxygen and give their numbers of protons and neutrons.

rubric.why: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
rubric.description: Defines isotopes using atomic number and mass number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both that the atomic number is the same and the mass number differs.

rubric.why: The commonly described carbon isotopes have mass numbers 12, 13 and 14.
rubric.description: Identifies the three carbon isotopes by mass number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly naming or giving the mass numbers of carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14.

rubric.why: The three hydrogen isotopes are protium, deuterium and tritium, with mass numbers 1, 2 and 3.
rubric.description: Names the three isotopes of hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming all three isotopes or giving their mass numbers.

rubric.why: The hydrogen isotopes contain zero, one and two neutrons, respectively.
rubric.description: Describes the neutron numbers of the hydrogen isotopes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly matching the three hydrogen isotopes to their neutron numbers.

rubric.why: The two common isotopes of chlorine have mass numbers 35 and 37.
rubric.description: Identifies the two common chlorine isotopes by mass number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving both chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.

modelAnswer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
Carbon has three isotopes: carbon-12 has 6 neutrons, carbon-13 has 7 neutrons and carbon-14 has 8 neutrons; each has 6 protons.
Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium (¹H) has 1 proton and 0 neutrons, deuterium (²H) has 1 proton and 1 neutron, and tritium (³H) has 1 proton and 2 neutrons.
Chlorine has two common isotopes: chlorine-35 has 17 protons and 18 neutrons, while chlorine-37 has 17 protons and 20 neutrons.
